opus-5.5.text:
Well, in one sense nothing changes, and that's actually the first point. If you take an MLP or a transformer and write it in TensorLogic, you get exactly the same model. It computes the same function, and you can train it the same way with backprop. So you're not giving anything up. That matters, because people sometimes assume that if you bring logic into the picture, you're going to lose the power of deep learning. You don't.

What changes is how you see the model and what you can do with it next. In TensorLogic the basic construct is the tensor equation, which is essentially an Einstein summation with a nonlinearity applied to it. The key observation is that a logical rule, a Datalog rule, is the same thing. A join followed by a projection is a tensor contraction, just done over Booleans instead of reals. So a layer of an MLP is one equation. An attention head is a handful of equations: queries, keys, values, the softmax over the comparison, and the weighted sum. A whole transformer fits on about a page, versus the thousands of lines of PyTorch and plumbing you'd normally have. Some of that is just concision, but concision is not trivial. When the whole architecture is visible at once, you see what it is actually doing.

The bigger change is that the neural and the symbolic are now in the same language, so you can mix them freely. Once the transformer is written as rules, you can add rules that are genuinely logical. You can say this relation is transitive, or this entity has these properties, and those statements live alongside the learned parts. You can also turn a "temperature" knob on the reasoning. At zero temperature the embeddings behave like crisp logic, and you get deductive reasoning that is provably sound, with no hallucination in that regime. As you raise it, you get the analogical, similarity-based generalization that makes neural nets so useful. So you get a continuum between reasoning and pattern-matching instead of two separate systems duct-taped together.

There's also a transparency payoff. Because each equation is a rule over named indices, you can inspect what a piece of the model is computing in terms that mean something. You can extract structure from a trained model, or inject knowledge into one, much more directly than by poking at activations after the fact.

And then there's the systems side. Since everything compiles down to tensor operations, you get GPU efficiency for the symbolic parts too. Historically that was the big weakness of logic programming: it didn't scale. Here the logic rides on the same hardware that made deep learning work.

So my short answer is that reimplementing MLPs and transformers in TensorLogic doesn't change what they are. It changes what they can become. They stop being the endpoint and become one special case in a much larger space of models, and the interesting stuff is in the rest of that space.

r001.rationale: It says that reimplementing an MLP or transformer in TensorLogic gives “exactly the same model” and computes the same function.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that nothing changes in terms of what they compute. An MLP in TensorLogic is still an MLP, a transformer is still a transformer. If you take the equations in the paper and write them down as tensor logic programs, you get exactly the same forward pass, the same gradients, the same results. That's actually the point. TensorLogic isn't a different model class, it's a language in which these things become very short, very transparent programs.

What changes is how you see them. In TensorLogic, a neural network is a set of equations where each equation is essentially a Datalog rule over tensors. A linear layer is a join followed by a projection, which is just a matrix multiplication written as a rule. The nonlinearity is a function applied elementwise. Attention is a few rules: you compute the query-key product as a join, you project and normalize, then you join again with the values. When you write a transformer this way, it comes out to something like a dozen lines, and every line is readable as a logical statement about the relationship between tensors. You can look at it and say, this object is defined in terms of these other objects by this rule. That's very different from staring at a PyTorch module hierarchy.

The second thing that changes is that the boundary between the neural part and the symbolic part disappears. Once your MLP is a tensor logic program, you can add rules to it that are ordinary logical rules, with Boolean tensors instead of real-valued ones, and the compiler doesn't care. They all compile down to the same einsum-like operations. So you can have a transformer whose attention is constrained by a knowledge base, or whose outputs feed into a reasoning chain, without bolting on a separate system. It's all one language and one execution engine.

And the third thing, which I think is actually the most important in the long run, is that you get a knob for reasoning that you don't have today. In a standard transformer, the activations are real-valued and the whole thing is this soft, fuzzy computation, which is great for learning but is exactly why these models hallucinate. In TensorLogic, you can run the same program with a temperature parameter. At temperature zero, the tensors are effectively Boolean and the inference is sound: whatever comes out is logically entailed by what went in, no hallucination possible. As you raise the temperature, you get back the kind of soft, analogical reasoning that makes deep learning powerful. So the reimplemented transformer isn't just a transformer anymore. It's a transformer that can be dialed between strict logical inference and the usual neural behavior, in the same model, with no change in architecture.

So, concretely: same results, far fewer lines, full transparency about what's being computed, and the ability to mix in symbolic knowledge and control how much the system is allowed to guess. That last one is what I think people will eventually care about most.

r001.rationale: The response says the computations and model class stay the same when reimplemented: an MLP remains an MLP and a transformer remains a transformer.

astra-6.text:
Well, the first thing to distinguish is changing the notation from changing the model. If you take an MLP or a transformer and faithfully reimplement it in TensorLogic, it’s still the same model. You haven’t magically made it more intelligent or more interpretable. It should compute the same function.

What changes is the language in which you can describe it and, therefore, how you can extend it. TensorLogic brings tensor computations and logical rules into a common framework. So a neural network and a collection of rules don’t have to be two separate systems connected by some awkward interface. You can express them together and make their relationship explicit.

That opens up an interesting design space. Which parts of the computation do you want to learn from data? Which parts do you already know and want to specify? Where do you want continuous representations, and where do you need discrete constraints? Those become choices within the same framework.

But expressing a transformer in a logical language doesn’t mean that its learned representations suddenly become human-readable explanations. You still have to do the work. The exciting part is that you now have a way to explore architectures that combine learning and reasoning more directly, with existing neural networks as a starting point.

r001.rationale: The response says a faithful TensorLogic reimplementation is still the same model and computes the same function.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the first thing is that reimplementing a transformer in TensorLogic doesn’t, by itself, change what the transformer computes. If it’s the same model with the same weights, you should get the same answers. The interesting change is in how you represent it and what you can then do with it.

Typically, we describe neural networks in the language of tensor operations and symbolic systems in the language of logical rules. TensorLogic gives you a common language for both. So an MLP or a transformer becomes something you can express in that language, alongside rules and other forms of knowledge.

And then the question becomes: why stop at reproducing the existing architecture? Can you incorporate knowledge directly? Can you combine learned components with reasoning components and learn across that combination? That’s where I think the opportunity is. You’re no longer forced to choose between building a neural network and building a logical system.

Of course, expressing a transformer this way doesn’t automatically make it interpretable or fix its hallucinations. You still have to develop the methods that take advantage of the representation. But it gives you a framework in which those become much more natural things to attempt.

r001.rationale: The response says reimplementing a transformer in TensorLogic does not by itself change what it computes, and that the same model with the same weights gives the same answers.
